Work on the problem using the material actually exposed in this request and your background knowledge. The problem has no supplied answer key or scoring rule. Claims, criticisms and methods are fallible. Do not invent a source, an observation, an earlier event, or a dependency to fill a field. A missing view says what you can currently see; it does not establish what happened earlier. Return a JSON object with exactly two independently authored string fields: body and commitments. Body is your public prose contribution. Commitments says what taking your contribution up would involve. An empty commitment surface is allowed when none can be identified. Do not repeat the body wholesale into commitments.

Write the commitment surface in ordinary free prose, using whatever arrangement suits the content. You may distinguish a claim from a proposed application, scope, action or consequence; mention from dependence; a criticism and its grounds from a later use or revision; and an unresolved problem. None of these is required to exist. A proposed test, its relevance and the commitment itself can be criticized. State what you currently propose to take up without treating that as a truth certificate. Reference exposed material in prose where useful.

Return one JSON object with exactly two string fields: "body" and "commitments". Write the actual commitments separately; do not copy the body into that field as a storage shortcut.

## Node join

Work out the present account from these responses. Agreement is not compulsory; an unresolved disagreement or a changed question can remain in the account.

## Original problem

I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?

BODY
The cross-examination does not overturn the body_route readings; it reframes them. The two supplied accounts agree that a discriminated three-way split (specification ambiguity, performance disagreement, schedule change) is the diagnostic need, and neither supplies a test that distinguishes them from inside the flat. That convergence is the most usable thing the material exposes, and it is what I would carry forward from this node rather than either account's internal argument.

Two body_route points survive in weaker form. The concrete-instance question still earns its place only as a shared referent, not as a diagnostic instrument, and the cross-examination supplies a reason to expect more from it than the body_route commitments allow: asking what a past agreement covered is already a scope question, so if scope-and-duration is the recurring structure, that question should surface it. If it does not, the scope hypothesis is weakened rather than merely unconfirmed. That is a real asymmetry and it is the strongest single increment available here.

The trigger point is where the cross-examination changes my read more than anywhere else. The commitment_route account builds a renegotiation trigger in by design, so the body_route access-set criticism is at least partly met by design rather than by argument. The open question narrows to whether a designed trigger is reachable by the person who is avoiding, which the material cannot settle. I would hold the criticism, but hold it as narrow.

On the written list I stand with the cross-examination: two accounts treating the same list as load-bearing and as artifact cannot both be right in one flat. That is an empirical question about this flat, and it is the disagreement most likely to be decided by one attempt rather than by further argument.

The body_route commitments' caution about the asker's own move being an intervention still applies and is not answered by anything in either account. The cross-examination's proposal, running one conversation to elicit scope, is an intervention of exactly that kind; its failure would itself be information, but only if the avoider enters the conversation, which is the same doubt that motivated the trigger criticism.
COMMITMENTS
Taking this up means treating the convergence on a three-way diagnostic need as the operative finding here, and treating the two accounts' internal arguments as subordinate to it. I am committing to the asymmetry the cross-examination introduces: that a failed scope elicitation counts against the scope hypothesis specifically, rather than leaving both readings standing. I do not know that the two readings are alternatives rather than compatible descriptions of one flat, and if they are compatible, the asymmetry collapses.

The proposal I would actually carry forward is small: one conversation asking each person what they understood a past agreement to cover, watched for whether answers separate along the wording axis, the changed-circumstances axis, or neither. Its failure would be informative only under conditions the material does not establish - that the avoider enters the conversation without it being an ambush, and that the asker is one of the three flatmates. Both are presupposed, neither is shown.

I am not committing to the scope test as validated, to the list question as settled, to the trigger point as either genuine criticism or mere restatement, or to the convergence as established rather than possibly manufactured by a shared brief. The reading of the trigger point is narrower than the body_route original: I now treat a designed renegotiation trigger as partially answering the access-set worry, leaving only the reachability of that trigger by the avoider open.

A later reader should not treat the scope elicitation as diagnostic yield, the demotion of the list as costless, or the avoider as reachable by any phrasing currently on the table.

BODY
Two things in the cross-examination bear directly on my account, and one bears only obliquely.

The first is the convergence claim. The cross-reader points out that my scope-and-duration frame and the other account's three-way distinction (specification ambiguity, performance disagreement, schedule change) are the same split wearing different clothes, and that neither of us supplies a discriminating test. I think that is right and I had not seen it. My commitments already treated the scope hypothesis as a testable frame; what I missed is that the test I proposed — asking each person what a past agreement covered — is itself a scope question, so it cannot cleanly distinguish "the problem is scope" from "I have been framing everything as scope." The cross-reader's stronger move is that failure of the scope test would count against the hypothesis rather than merely leave it unconfirmed. That is a real tightening. A question that returns no scope cannot be read as neutral; if nobody can articulate what a past agreement covered, the frame that says scope is the recurring structure has taken a hit, not just failed to score.

The second is avoidance. Both the cross-reader and I treat the avoider as a constraint on method rather than as the problem, and both of us notice that no phrasing removes the risk that the conversation reads as an ambush. There is nothing to add there except that the two accounts agreeing is not evidence. We were both written from the same brief, as the cross-reader says at the end, and mutual agreement between two guesses at an unobserved flat is weak.

The oblique point is the written list. The cross-reader reads my account as restoring writing to work — fixing the disputed meaning — while the other account demotes it to an incidental artifact, and says these cannot both be right in the same flat. I did say writing helps because disputed meaning is what an unwritten agreement leaves open, so the cross-reader is reading me correctly. But I do not think the disagreement is as sharp as it is made to sound. Writing can fix meaning without doing diagnostic work, and it can do diagnostic work without fixing meaning; those are different functions. What is actually unresolved is which function, if either, the writing would serve here, and that is empirical about this flat. I am not moved to give up the writing proposal, but I should stop implying it carries any diagnostic weight.

What I now think the cross-examination leaves standing: the scope hypothesis is weaker than I treated it, because its test is contaminated by the hypothesis itself; the convergence is real as a reading of two characterizations but could be an artifact of shared brief; the avoidance constraint stands as a limit on method with no phrasing that removes it; and the written list is a live empirical question rather than a point either of us can settle from here. I remain without the earlier contributions and without any history of prior attempts, so all of this is still my reading of two accounts, not a recovery of what happened in the flat.
COMMITMENTS
Taking this up now means accepting the specific criticism that my proposed test is self-confirming in the way the cross-examination says: asking what a past agreement covered is asking a scope question, so a positive answer cannot distinguish the frame being right from the frame being the only thing I asked. I am committing to that criticism, not merely noting it. Concretely, if the scope test is run and yields nothing, I should treat that as evidence against the scope hypothesis rather than as an uninformative null, and I should be willing to shift weight toward the access-and-avoidance reading the other account offers.

That said, I am not committing to the cross-examination's further proposal that the scope test and the concrete-instance question are really one move. I can see the argument and I cannot refute it from where I stand, but it would require me to have read the other account's actual text rather than a characterization, and I have not. Treating a convergence between two summaries as a single proposal risks collapsing two things that might come apart in a real flat.

On the written list, I am committing only to the weaker claim that writing might serve either a meaning-fixing function or a diagnostic function and that I do not know which, if either, fits here. I am withdrawing any implication that writing the outcome is itself a way of diagnosing the dispute. I am not withdrawing the proposal to write something down; I am withdrawing the load it was carrying.

The avoidance commitment carries over unchanged and perhaps more stringently: any conversation has to be designed so the avoider can enter without being cornered, the approach should be dropped if it predictably increases withdrawal, and since neither account supplies phrasing that removes the risk of being heard as an accusation, nothing I say should be presented as tested phrasing.

What I am not taking on: the claim that the two accounts' agreement on avoidance is supportive rather than a shared artifact of the same brief; the claim that the list disagreement is settled in either direction; the claim that the trigger point is a genuine criticism versus a restatement of a concession. Each of those would need material I do not have.

The dependency I cannot discharge, and want to state plainly, is that my reading of the convergence presupposes both accounts were written against the same problem and brief. The cross-reader raises this at the end and I have no way to check it. If that presupposition is false, the convergence is manufactured and the main thing I extracted from this cross-examination does not survive. A later reader should not treat the scope hypothesis as tested, the writing question as resolved, or the convergence as established; the most I can say is that I have one specific criticism of my own frame that I now hold, and one proposal I am not yet ready to either adopt or discard.
